lines.text: Driving in Britain has unique characteristics that distinguish it from most other countries. The most obvious is driving on the left — a tradition dating back centuries, now shared by only about 35% of the world's countries. The steering wheel is on the right-hand side of the vehicle. Speed limits are measured in miles per hour: 30 mph in built-up areas, 60 mph on single carriageways, and 70 mph on dual carriageways and motorways. The Highway Code — a comprehensive guide to road rules, signs, and best practice — is essential reading for all road users and is regularly updated. Roundabouts are a defining feature of British road design — circular junctions where traffic flows clockwise, with priority given to vehicles already on the roundabout. The driving test consists of a theory test (multiple-choice questions and hazard perception) followed by a practical test lasting approximately 40 minutes. Learner drivers must display L-plates (red 'L' on white background) and can only drive with a qualified accompanying driver. After passing, new drivers receive a full licence but remain on probation — accumulating six points within two years means the licence is revoked. Speed cameras — both fixed and mobile — enforce limits across the road network. Penalty points, fines, and driving bans are issued for offences including speeding, using a mobile phone while driving, drink-driving, and running red lights.
